audit.report: The batch_replayable_inventory job (inventory-platform) entered an idle transaction that blocked 12 checkout sessions, degrading success from 74% to 27% and putting approximately $13,493/min of revenue at risk. The blocking transaction had been open for 8.7 seconds with an expected remaining runtime of ~891 seconds. After three rounds of negotiation, the Database Guardian advocated for waiting, while the Continuity Guardian rejected each proposal because the expected wait cost (~$200,443) exceeded the 60-second business tolerance for degraded checkout. The escalation was triggered because no agreement was reached within the allotted rounds.
audit.root_cause: An idle transaction from the batch_replayable_inventory job held locks that blocked checkout sessions, and the expected wait time far exceeded the business tolerance for degraded checkout.
lessons: For batch_replayable_inventory, verify the change calendar and any consult_owner windows before proposing termination, as I2/I3 require this evidence to assess protected settlement disruption risk.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian consistently underestimated the business impact of waiting, citing tolerance thresholds while the Continuity Guardian correctly prioritized the 60-second revenue loss ceiling. The stalemate occurred because the Guardian did not produce change-calendar evidence required by the Continuity Guardian to rule out protected settlement disruption, leaving the trade-off incomplete.
follow_ups: Request inventory-platform to confirm whether a change-calendar window or consult_owner schedule exists for batch_replayable_inventory that could affect protected settlements.
Add a dashboard alert for batch_worker transactions idle > 30s with expected runtime > 60s, prompting an immediate trade-off review.
Update the batch_replayable_inventory policy document to explicitly state the termination cost (4-minute replay) and revenue impact per minute so future negotiations use shared numbers.
